title: Hello, I'm from Indonesia
goal: Greet anyone safely, give your name and where you're from, ask the other person the same, and recognize the two polite forms used throughout this module.
bekal: greet with 안녕하세요 at any time, day or night
say your nationality and your job
tell the 입니다 form apart from the 이에요/예요 form
say goodbye with the right word depending on who is leaving

dialogs.title: 대화 — First day of language class
dialogs.intro: Ani, a student from Indonesia, sits down next to a stranger in a Korean class in Seoul. Notice that neither of them ever says the word "you".

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.literal: I — as-for — Ani — am. name — subject — what — is?

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.literal: my — name — as-for — Kim Minjun — is (formal).

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.literal: Minjun — Mr. — as-for — Korea — person — is?

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Yes, I'm Korean. And you, Ani?
lines.literal: yes, Korea — person — am. Ani — Ms. — as-for — (then)?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.literal: I — as-for — Korea — person — subject — not-am. Indonesia — person — am.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Oh, really? Are you a student?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. Are you a student too, Minjun?
lines.literal: yes, student — am. Minjun — Mr. — also — student — are?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. I look forward to working with you.

notes: **안녕하세요 has no clock.** There's no separate "good morning", "good afternoon" and "good evening" as in English. This one word works from dawn to midnight, with anyone. Literally it means "are you at peace?" — which is why it's a question, even though the tone falls like a statement.

**Korean avoids the word "you".** There isn't a single second-person pronoun in the dialogue above. Instead people use **name + 씨**: 민준 씨는…? Calling someone 당신 ("you") can sound like you're picking a fight, even though old textbooks often list it. Delete that word from your head right now.

**씨 goes with names, not titles.** 민준 씨 is safe between adults of equal standing. But ⚠️ don't use 씨 with your boss or teacher — use their title instead: 선생님 (teacher), 사장님 (company president). Calling your boss by name + 씨 is as awkward as calling the dean by a nickname.

**저 and 나 both mean "I".** 저 is the humble form, and it's the one used in this module; 나 is the plain form, safe only among close friends your own age. With the topic particle attached it becomes 저는, and "my" is 제 (not 저의).

**씨는요? lets you bounce the question back without repeating it.** The ending 요 attached to a particle means "what about…?". It's very common and very handy: whenever someone asks you something, answer and then turn it around with 씨는요?

**아니요 means "no" as an answer; 아니에요 means "is not" as a verb.** Two similar words that are easily mixed up. 아니요 stands alone at the start of a sentence; 아니에요 ends the sentence and needs a noun with the particle 이/가 before it: 한국 사람**이** 아니에요.

**Goodbye has two forms, and what decides it is who is moving.** 안녕히 **가**세요 ("go in peace") is said to the person who is **leaving**. 안녕히 **계**세요 ("stay in peace") is said to the person who is **staying**. If you're both leaving, you both say 안녕히 가세요. Picking the wrong one instantly marks you as a foreigner.

**잘 부탁합니다 has no real English equivalent.** Literally "please treat me well", it's said at the start of any relationship: a new class, a new office, a new team. It isn't empty politeness — leaving it out of a formal introduction actually feels cold.

grammars.title: 이에요 / 예요 — "to be"
body: The first verb you must master. It attaches **directly to the end** of the noun with no space, and its form depends on the last letter of that noun.
after: The reason is simply ease of pronunciation: after a consonant you need a linking vowel, after a vowel you don't. This "vowel or consonant" rule comes back with almost every Korean particle, so get into the habit now of checking the last letter of the noun.
The question form is **exactly the same**; only the intonation rises at the end: 학생이에요. (statement) and 학생이에요? (question). Korean doesn't flip word order to ask a question.
The negative doesn't attach; it's a separate word, **아니에요**, and the noun before it takes the particle 이/가: 학생**이** 아니에요 (is not a student), 의사**가** 아니에요 (is not a doctor).

grammars.title: Two politeness levels used throughout the module
body: The same sentence takes different shapes depending on who you're talking to. At A1 you only need to recognize two, and only one needs to be drilled until it's automatic.
after: **This module uses 해요체 as its main form** because that's what you'll use ninety percent of the time. 합쇼체 is introduced so you can recognize it in station announcements and on the news, not so you drill it.

What you must not use with people you've just met is **반말** — the casual form without 요 that you hear in TV dramas: 아니야, 어디 가? It sounds natural between characters who are friends, and rude from a foreigner who has only just met someone. Wait until the other person offers it.
⚠️ Note that 감사합니다 and 안녕하세요 are used as they are at both levels. Both have frozen into fixed words and don't need to change.

sections.title: Words to have in your pocket on day one

blocks.text: The eleven expressions below cover most of the small talk on your first day. Learn them whole and don't take their grammar apart yet — everything will be explained in due course.

head: 한국어
Romanization
English
rows: How do you say it in Korean?

blocks.text: The last two sentences are learning tools, not just vocabulary. Once you can ask "what's this?" and "how do you say it in Korean?", every Korean around you becomes a walking dictionary.

blocks.title: 죄송합니다 vs 실례합니다
items: **죄송합니다** is used when you're genuinely at fault: bumping into someone, arriving late, making a mistake.
**실례합니다** is used when you're about to inconvenience someone a little: interrupting a conversation, passing in front of someone, asking a stranger in the street.
Using 죄송합니다 just to get past someone sounds over the top; using 실례합니다 after spilling coffee on someone's shirt sounds clueless.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Korean. Use the 해요체 form.
Fill in 이에요 or 예요 according to the last letter of the noun.
Put the words in the right order.
Choose the right expression. Write your answer in hangeul.
items: You meet your teacher in the hallway at seven in the morning. You say ____.
Your friend leaves the café first; you're staying. You say ____.
You're leaving the office; your coworker is still working. You say ____.
You accidentally bump into someone on the train. You say ____.
You want to pass in front of someone who is sitting down. You say ____.

answers: 안녕하세요. — 저는 아니예요. — 저는 인도네시아 사람이에요. — 이름이 뭐예요? — 저는 학생이에요. — 저는 회사원이 아니에요.
